prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which established moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: I keep B013 as my preferred sole prize part, and the first round has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The claim being rewarded is narrow and testable: a simple continuum model (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) predicted that the moire of two graphene sheets produces nearly flat bands at a magic angle, and the 2018 experiments showed that this tunable carbon system hosts correlated insulating and superconducting states. Neither half depends on a settled pairing mechanism. The flat band is a band-structure fact that scanning-tunnelling and other spectroscopic measurements have since checked against calculation, and the correlated phases have been reproduced by many independent groups and carried into twisted multilayers and TMD moire systems. For a theorist that is the right closure: a quantitative prediction, a measurement that could have failed, and a new platform that other labs now use. It is also a surprise of the kind I value, since a material long regarded as weakly correlated turned out to host strongly correlated physics from one control knob. I would word the citation so that it credits the prediction of the flat band and the discovery of the phases, not a particular sample or a mechanism.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are timing and attribution. The experiments are under a decade old, the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, and sample dependence (twist-angle disorder, strain, substrate) is large. Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and earlier band-structure work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and by Suarez Morell and colleagues, lie outside the three credited names. I cannot settle the priority record from the files I am allowed to use, and I will not claim more certainty than I have. B061 is the more mature candidate in the plain sense: a longer record, direct cross-continental comparisons, and a clean two-name attribution. If the committee decides that a settled mechanism or a decade of consolidation is required, B061 is the better prize this year, and I would accept it.

responses.point: Kroll calls the lattice clock an engineering-physics achievement rather than a new phenomenon, proposes narrow wording for the invention and realisation of the lattice clock, and holds that the pending SI redefinition of the second should not count in the timing.
responses.response: Your own candour about the discovery content is what moves me most, and it answers the question I put to you in round 1. I agree with you that the redefinition should not drive a physics prize. On the novelty question the chair put to you, I think your narrow wording does meet the 2005 and 2012 objection for the lattice idea itself, since magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a different principle from single-ion control. But the narrower you make the citation, the more it describes a method, and the more B013's appeal grows by contrast: a new state of matter and a prediction checked by experiment. I still rank B013 first. I also say plainly that your reproducibility argument is stronger than anything I can offer for the graphene superconductivity, and that I could vote for B061 if the committee puts maturity first.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks, that the redefinition of the second is a consequence and not a motivation, and that two names leave out real contributors such as Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley and Takamoto.
responses.response: I accept your distinction between the lattice principle and the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes; it is fair, and it is why I keep B061 as my first alternative and not a distant one. Your credit-boundary worry is, however, the same as mine for B013, and I think we should treat them even-handedly. Both prizes would draw a line through a field with strong contributors outside it, and neither argument by itself disqualifies the other. The difference I see is that for B013 the line separates a prediction from its experimental discovery, which gives two natural claimants, while for B061 the line runs through a group of laboratories reaching similar accuracy at similar times. That seems to me a somewhat harder boundary to defend for the clocks, but I hold that view loosely because I am outside your field.

responses.point: Olsson asks for certainty about the original credit in B013 before settling and wants the citation to credit the discovery of the phases and not individual samples.
responses.response: I agree with that wording rule and have used it in my citation. On the factual question, I can say what I have and no more. The prediction credit for the continuum model rests with Bistritzer and MacDonald, and I am confident that earlier band-structure studies anticipated that the bands narrow at small twist angles but did not give the magic-angle mechanism and its quantitative control. For the experiment I cannot rule out that omitting Yuan Cao, or the contemporaneous groups, is unacceptable. Like you, I would not push a three-name citation if the committee finds that the record cannot support it. In that case I would prefer to move to B061 and not to alter B013 by adding or removing names, because the three-person limit leaves no room to add Cao.

responses.point: Mehlig thinks B013 is strong but early, that B008 or B061 are safer if the pairing mechanism must be understood first, and asks whether the committee will accept a prize before the mechanism is known.
responses.response: I take the question seriously and my answer is yes, with a stated condition. Nobel recognition has often gone to a discovery of a phenomenon or phase before its microscopic origin was agreed, and the rewarded claim here is the flat band and the existence of tunable correlated phases. What would settle the question for me is that the phases are reproduced independently across platforms, which they have been, and that the citation says nothing about the pairing mechanism. What would change my mind is evidence that the correlated states depend on a particular sample preparation, or that the flat-band picture fails quantitatively in cleaner devices; I do not know of such evidence. I would not follow you to B008, for the reasons I gave in round 1: it rewards an idea spread across many fields and loses a co-originator.

uncertainties: Whether the historical record supports a three-name citation that leaves out Yuan Cao and the contemporaneous experimental groups; I rely on memory of the 2018 papers and cannot check priority from the permitted files.
Whether the committee considers it acceptable to reward B013 before the pairing mechanism is understood, or wants a longer period of independent consolidation.
Whether a second condensed-matter prize after the 2016 topological-phases prize and the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits should tip the committee toward B061 this year.
Whether the 10^-18 lattice-clock result, outside my own field, is a distinct principle or a third step in the 2005 and 2012 line; I defer to Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce on that.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen since round 1. I work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism and have no known personal, institutional or collaborative link to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I have no connection to the clock community, and I would stay out of any B018 or B002 discussion where colleagues have disclosed ties.
